title: Hearing Art Tatum as a student in Louisville
summary: He places his first meeting with Tatum in the late 1920s when Art was a student, and recalls Earl Hines's amazed expression in Chicago.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: Art Tatum was an influence on you, although you didn't try to copy him...You had said also that you heard him for the first time in Louisville.

He was going to school. Art originally...was going around playing in...well, ...Art, during the early years, was a student. And he was quite unusual, and he used to go around various sections of the country and play in piano appearances with colleges, you know, and competitions. So that's as nearly as I can recall to my first meeting with him was that he was in that category. Now there's a professional performer. So that's ......... first knew him. But really to know him, was in Chicago when Lovey Taylor told Earl Hines there was a kid in the house that could play the piano and he play "Tiger Rag," you know, like a shotgun. I mean that...I've never seen an expression...well, I saw one other expression on Earl Hines' face, you know what I mean, it was like a thing of amazement. That was when we were going to Europe in 1948 with Louis Armstrong--he was with Louis, you know--and there were several bands going for that International Festival in Nice and Earl Hines and Jack Teagarden and Sid Catlett and Barney Bigard and Arvell Shaw and Velma Middleton, Louis, and...who was playing trombone... in that band?
